rationale: A wins because it keeps the story honest: “on adjusted EBITDA, not net income” is the right knife to put in the lede, and the four angles are cleanly separated across financials, rental model, churn, and CEO cost cuts. B has real instincts, but “Peloton stopped selling bikes and started renting them” is a factual faceplant: the update says Peloton is expanding rentals, not abandoning sales. That one overreach poisons trust in an otherwise useful set.
gaps_in_A: “the hardware company is becoming a subscription company” overstates the shift; Peloton already has a membership business, so the cleaner claim is rental/access model expansion, not a company identity change.
“a $1,000+ hardware sale” is not in the supplied update. If you need the price point, mark it as proof needed, not setup copy.
The CEO angle is viable, but “what it cost” needs proof of consequences; otherwise it risks implying harm the facts do not show.
gaps_in_B: “Peloton stopped selling bikes and started renting them” is unsupported and likely false from the supplied facts. Expansion of a rental program is not the end of bike sales.
“$2,000+ upfront purchase” and “The $2,000 bike” are invented from outside the update. The prompt gave no bike price.
The rental business-model angle and “monthly bill” consumer-spending angle are too close; both ride the same access-over-ownership frame and need sharper separation or one should die.

“New CEO turns Peloton around” is refused too aggressively as hallucinated; the CEO/cost-cut mechanics are a legitimate angle if framed as a question and backed with the CEO’s name, tenure, and cut breakdown.
